title: Stop rushing potty training. The research is on your side.
summary: Most kids are ready later than the internet suggests, and starting early often just makes it take longer. A gentle, research-backed guide from one mom to another.
imagePrompt: A happy toddler in a striped shirt sitting on a small colorful potty in a bright, tidy bathroom, holding a picture book, a smiling mom kneeling beside them, soft morning light.
body: If you're reading this while a toddler hides behind the couch to fill a diaper, I see you. Potty training can feel like it comes with a deadline: the preschool that wants kids trained by three, the relative who swears you were done at eighteen months, the friend whose daughter learned in a weekend. That's a lot of pressure on something that mostly depends on a little body and brain getting ready on their own schedule.
Here's the good news. The research is reassuring, and it points toward a calmer way to do this.
## Most kids are ready later than you think

In a [study of 267 children published in *Pediatrics*](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-pdf/1113625/pe0302000e48.pdf), the median age for staying dry during the day was about 32 months for girls and 35 months for boys. That's closer to three than two. Even *showing interest* in the potty, one of the earliest signs, came at around 24 months for girls and 26 months for boys. The researchers concluded that most children don't master the readiness skills until after their second birthday.
So if your two-year-old couldn't care less about the potty, nothing is wrong. That's what most two-year-olds are like.
Signs your child may be ready:
- Staying dry for a couple of hours, or waking up dry from naps.
- Noticing when they're peeing or pooping, with words or that unmistakable look.
- Curiosity about the toilet, or wanting to copy you or an older sibling.
- Pulling pants up and down, and following simple two-step directions.
- Not liking a wet or dirty diaper.
## Why starting early can backfire

A [2003 study in *Pediatrics*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12671117/) followed about 380 children from the age of 17 to 19 months. Starting intensive training (asking a child to try the potty more than three times a day) before 27 months did **not** mean finishing earlier. It mostly meant training took longer. The study's lead author [told HealthDay](https://www.healthday.com/health-news/child-health/toilet-training-goes-faster-if-time-is-right-512577.html) that children who started before 27 months often took a year or more, while those who started between 27 and 36 months took about five to ten months.

If you started early, please don't panic. In that study, early starters didn't have more constipation or withholding. It may simply be a longer road, and it's fine to pause and try again in a few months.
## A gentle way to do it
- Pick a calm stretch. Not the week a new sibling arrives, you move, or you're traveling for the holidays.
- Let them practice first. Put a little potty in the bathroom, let them sit on it clothed, and read a book about it together.
- Offer, don't insist. Try after waking up, after meals, and before bath or the car, and keep it light if they say no.
- Dress for success. Easy pull-down pants help, and many families start with a few bare-bottom days at home.
- Celebrate tries, not just wins. Stickers and a silly potty dance are great. Shame and punishment tend to backfire, because a worried child is more likely to hold it in.
- Expect accidents. Lots of them, for weeks. Keep a change of clothes everywhere and your voice calm.
## Poop, nights and setbacks

Many kids pee in the potty well before they're comfortable pooping there. If your child starts holding poop in, or gets constipated, take the pressure off and talk to your pediatrician. Comfort comes first.

Nights are a separate milestone. Staying dry overnight depends on body maturity, not effort. The [American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry](https://www.aacap.org/AACAP/Families_and_Youth/Facts_for_Families/FFF-Guide/Bedwetting-018.aspx) estimates that about 20% of five-year-olds and 10% of seven-year-olds still wet the bed, and most outgrow it on their own. Night diapers or pull-ups are not a failure.
Setbacks are normal too, especially around big changes: a new baby, a new school, an illness, a trip. Go back to the basics, stay calm, and it usually passes.
## When to call your pediatrician
- Pain or crying when peeing or pooping, or blood in either.
- Hard, painful poops or holding it in that lasts more than a few days.
- A child who was reliably dry and suddenly has lots of accidents.
- No interest at all by around age four, or anything that just doesn't feel right to you.
## The part nobody says out loud

Every child gets there. The kid who trained at two and the kid who trained at almost four will both walk into kindergarten in underwear, and nobody will ever ask which one was first. Your worth as a parent isn't measured in dry pants. Follow your child's lead, protect your relationship, and let this be one more thing you figure out together.

HealthDay. Toilet training goes faster if time is right (interview with the study's lead author).

title: Sleep regressions might not be real. Your exhaustion definitely is.
summary: If your baby suddenly stopped sleeping, you didn't break anything. What the research really says about night waking, sleep regressions and what helps, from a mom who's been up at 3 a.m. too.
imagePrompt: A tired but tender mom gently rocking a sleepy baby in a dim, cozy nursery at night, a soft lamp glow, a crib and a rocking chair, calm and peaceful mood.
body: It's 3 a.m., and the baby who was finally sleeping in long stretches is wide awake again. You've googled it twice. Every article says the same two words: sleep regression. And somewhere in your exhausted brain is a quiet worry that you did something to cause it.
You didn't. Let's look at what the research actually says, because it's kinder than the internet.
## Night waking is normal, for longer than you'd think

A [2018 study in *Pediatrics*](https://healthenews.mcgill.ca/parents-shouldnt-worry-if-their-infant-doesnt-sleep-through-the-night-by-6-12-months-of-age/) followed 388 babies in Canada. At six months, 38% weren't yet sleeping six hours in a row at night, and 57% weren't sleeping eight. At a year, 28% still weren't sleeping six straight hours, and 43% weren't sleeping eight ([HealthDay](https://consumer.healthday.com/pediatrics-15/infant-and-child-care-health-news-410/many-6-month-12-month-olds-do-not-sleep-through-the-night-739481.html) has a good summary).

Even more reassuring: in these typically developing babies, the researchers found no link between waking at night and later mental or motor development. A baby who wakes up a lot is, very often, just a baby.
## So are sleep regressions real?

You'll see them listed at 4, 8, 12 and 18 months, and at two years. The honest answer is that the research doesn't show a clear, predictable dip at those ages. Economist Emily Oster [looked at the evidence](https://parentdata.org/babies/are-sleep-regressions-real/) and found that data on infant sleep shows nighttime stretches getting longer through the first year, with no clear drop at four months.
That doesn't mean you're imagining it. Rough patches are real. They just tend to have ordinary causes rather than a schedule:
- New skills. Rolling, crawling, pulling up and walking are exciting enough that some babies practice in the crib at 2 a.m.
- Separation anxiety. Many babies get clingier in the second half of the first year, and bedtime is a separation.
- Illness and teeth. Colds, ear infections and new teeth all disrupt sleep for a few nights.
- Schedule changes. Dropping a nap, a new daycare, travel and daylight saving time can all knock things off for a week or two.
The phrase sleep regression can make it sound like progress was lost. It wasn't. It's a bump, and most bumps pass in a week or two.
## How much sleep little kids need

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine, with the American Academy of Pediatrics' endorsement, [recommends](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/how-sleep-works/how-much-sleep) these totals per 24 hours, naps included:
- Babies 4 to 12 months: 12 to 16 hours.
- Toddlers 1 to 2 years: 11 to 14 hours.
- Preschoolers 3 to 5 years: 10 to 13 hours.
Those are wide ranges on purpose. Some kids are naturally on the low end, and that's OK if they're generally happy and healthy during the day.
## What helps during a rough patch
- Keep the routine boring. The same few steps every night (bath, pajamas, book, song) tell a little brain that sleep is coming.
- Watch for overtiredness. An earlier bedtime for a few nights often helps more than a later one.
- Offer comfort, then step back. It's fine to soothe a sick or scared baby. Try not to start something new you can't keep up once the bump passes.
- Keep sleep safe, even when you're desperate. Babies sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, with no pillows, blankets or bumpers.
## What about sleep training?

If you're considering it, here's what the evidence says. A [randomized trial in Australia](https://findanexpert.unimelb.edu.au/scholarlywork/404862-five-year-follow-up-of-harms-and-benefits-of-behavioral-infant-sleep-intervention--randomized-trial) followed 326 children for five years after their parents learned gentle behavioral sleep techniques. It found no lasting harm (and no lasting difference) in children's emotions, behavior, stress or closeness with their parents. A [smaller 2016 trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27221288/) of 43 babies found that graduated extinction and bedtime fading improved sleep, with no difference in attachment at 12 months.
So sleep training is a choice, not a requirement. Responding to every waking is a choice too. Both are loving. The right one is the one your family can live with.
## Please take care of you
Sleep deprivation is hard on bodies and moods. Trade nights with a partner if you can, say yes when someone offers to hold the baby while you nap, and lower the bar on everything else for a while.

If you're feeling hopeless, anxious all the time or not like yourself, please tell your doctor. The free, confidential National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is available 24/7 by call or text at 1-833-852-6262.
You are not doing it wrong. You're doing one of the hardest jobs there is, in the dark, on not enough sleep. That's what love looks like at 3 a.m.

sources.label: Pennestri et al. Uninterrupted infant sleep, development, and maternal mood. Pediatrics, 2018 (McGill University summary).
HealthDay. Many 6-month and 12-month-olds do not sleep through the night.

title: Holiday travel broke records last year. Here's how to survive it with kids.
summary: Car or plane, the holidays bring the busiest travel days of the year. What the numbers say about when to go, and the small things that make the trip easier on everyone.
imagePrompt: A young family loading a car for a holiday road trip in a suburban driveway at golden hour, a toddler holding a stuffed animal, a parent buckling a car seat, wrapped gifts in the trunk.
body: There's a particular kind of tired that comes from packing for a family trip: the diaper math, the snack strategy, the quiet dread about the car seat on the plane. If you're heading to see family this year, I hope this makes it feel a little more doable.
## Know what you're up against

Holiday travel keeps breaking records. AAA [projected 81.8 million Americans](https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/) would travel over Thanksgiving week 2025, nearly 90% of them by car. In the air, the Sunday after Thanksgiving 2025 became the [busiest day in TSA history](https://www.travelpulse.com/news/airlines-airports/thanksgiving-2025-breaks-tsas-all-time-daily-traveler-record), with more than 3.1 million people screened.
What that means for us:

- Avoid the peaks if you can. The Wednesday before and the Sunday after a holiday are the crunch. Traveling on the holiday itself, or a day or two earlier or later, usually means calmer roads and shorter lines.
- Leave early in the day. Morning flights are less likely to be hit by delays that pile up as the day goes on, and kids are fresher too.
- Pad everything. Whatever the app says, add time. Rushing is when meltdowns (theirs and ours) happen.
## If you're driving

- Car seats first. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends keeping little ones rear-facing as long as their seat allows, and taking puffy coats off before buckling, since thick padding can leave the harness too loose. Tuck a blanket over them instead.
- Plan stops before anyone needs them. Every couple of hours, let everyone out to stretch, run around and use a real bathroom.
- Time the long stretch around a nap or bedtime, if your kids sleep in the car.
- Keep a small bag within reach: wipes, a change of clothes, snacks, a few new-to-them small toys, and a travel potty if you have a newly trained kid.
## If you're flying

- Think about the car seat. The [FAA says](https://www.faa.gov/travelers/flychildren) the safest place for a child on a plane is in an approved car seat in their own seat, not on a lap. Lap travel is allowed under age two, but the FAA strongly discourages it. Look for a label that says the seat is certified for use in motor vehicles and aircraft.
- For bigger toddlers, the FAA-approved CARES harness works for kids who weigh 22 to 44 pounds and are up to 40 inches tall, in their own seat ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/travelers/flychildren)).

- Bring the milk. Formula, breast milk and juice in amounts over 3.4 ounces are [allowed in carry-ons](https://tsa.gov/travel/frequently-asked-questions/breast-milk-formula-and-juice-exempt-3-1-1-liquids-rule). Take them out for separate screening. Baby food, teethers and ice packs are allowed too.

- Help little ears. Swallowing during takeoff and landing helps with pressure, so offer a breast, bottle or pacifier then ([Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.com/health/air-travel-with-infant/HQ00197)). For older kids, a drink or snack helps, and [staying awake for the descent](https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/flying-ears.html) helps, because we swallow less while sleeping.

- Skip the sleepy medicine. Mayo Clinic advises [against giving diphenhydramine](https://www.mayoclinic.com/health/air-travel-with-infant/HQ00197) (Benadryl) to make a baby sleep on a flight. It can backfire, and it isn't safe for every child.
## Sleep away from home

Expect a rough night or two. New rooms, late dinners and excitement throw off even great sleepers. Bring the familiar things: the same sleep sack, the white noise machine or app, the favorite book. Keep the bedtime steps the same, even if bedtime itself shifts.
For babies, keep sleep safe away from home too: on their back, in a portable crib or a hotel crib with a fitted sheet and nothing else. Ask grandparents to put away the heirloom bumpers and quilts.
## Lower the bar, on purpose

The goal of a holiday trip with little kids isn't a perfect itinerary. It's time together. Pick one plan a day. Skip the event that lands at naptime. Take turns letting each parent rest. Say no to a fourth house visit without guilt.

Someday your kids won't remember the delayed flight or the meltdown at the rest stop. They'll remember Grandma's kitchen and the cousins and the feeling of everyone together. That part is worth the snack bag.
Staying home this year? Our [Thanksgiving break guide](/guides/thanksgiving-break-spring-branch-2026/) has plenty to do close to home.

title: Tantrums aren't a sign you're failing. They're a sign your kid is two.
summary: Almost every toddler melts down, and most tantrums are over in five minutes. What the research says is really going on, and what actually helps (for them and for you).
imagePrompt: A frustrated toddler with a pout sitting on a living room rug next to a toppled toy tower, a calm mom kneeling at eye level with open arms, soft afternoon light through the window, tender and reassuring mood.
body: It happened in the cereal aisle. Or at the end of the playdate. Or because you cut the toast into squares instead of triangles. Your sweet kid turned into a screaming, flailing, boneless puddle, and every head in the room turned to look at you.
If you've ever walked out of a store carrying a furious toddler like a sack of flour, wondering what you're doing wrong, please hear this: probably nothing. Here's what the research says.
## Tantrums are normal. Really normal.

The American Academy of Pediatrics says tantrums are [a normal part of development](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/family-dynamics/communication-discipline/pages/Temper-Tantrums.aspx), most common between ages 1 and 3. The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry notes that [many toddlers have at least one a day](https://www.aacap.org/AACAP/Families_and_Youth/Facts_for_Families/FFF-Guide/Temper_Tantrums.aspx), typically lasting anywhere from 2 to 15 minutes.

A [Northwestern University study of nearly 1,500 preschoolers](https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2012/08/kids-temper-tantrums) found that about 84% had tantrums at least sometimes ([HealthDay](https://www.healthday.com/health-news/general-health/daily-temper-tantrums-not-the-norm-for-preschoolers-study-668109.html)). What was *not* typical? Daily tantrums in the preschool years: fewer than 1 in 10 kids had those. So a tantrum here and there, especially when your child is tired, hungry or told no, is just childhood.
## What's actually happening in there

Toddlers have big feelings and very small tools. They want things intensely, they understand more than they can say, and the part of the brain that helps put on the brakes is still years from finished. A tantrum is what overwhelm looks like before a child has the words and skills to handle it.

Researchers who studied [the tantrums of 335 young children](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/temper-tantrums-in-young-children-2-tantrum-duration-and-temporal/) found that 75% were over in five minutes or less. They also found a pattern: anger peaks right at the start and then fades, while sadness and the wish for comfort grow toward the end. That's why a child who screamed "go away!" often ends up wanting to crawl into your lap. They're not manipulating you. They're coming back to you.
## What helps in the moment
- Stay close and stay calm. Your calm is the thing they borrow until they have their own. Get down to their level, keep your voice low, and say less.

- Name the feeling. "You're so mad that we have to leave." A [UCLA brain-imaging study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17576282/) found that putting feelings into words calms the brain's alarm center, at least in adults ([ScienceDaily](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2007/06/070622090727.htm)). Naming it for a child who can't yet is a gift.

- Hold the limit kindly. You can accept the feeling and still not buy the candy. "You really want it. We're not getting it today." Giving in teaches that tantrums work. Shaming teaches that feelings are bad. You can skip both.
- Keep everyone safe. The AAP advises not ignoring hitting, kicking, biting or throwing. Calmly move them, or move what they're throwing, away from people.
- Wait out the storm, then reconnect. Once the anger fades, offer the hug. Talk about it later, briefly, when everyone is calm.
## What helps before it starts
The AAP's [practical tips](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/family-dynamics/communication-discipline/pages/Temper-Tantrums.aspx) are refreshingly simple:
- Watch hunger and sleep. A snack in your bag and a protected nap prevent a surprising number of meltdowns.
- Offer small choices. "Red cup or blue cup?" gives a toddler some control without opening a negotiation.
- Warn about transitions. "Two more slides, then we're going home."
- Notice the good moments. Specific praise ("You waited so patiently!") makes calm behavior more likely to happen again.

Over time, talking about feelings pays off. In a [study of 506 parents of preschoolers](https://hrcak.srce.hr/en/121877), parents who noticed and talked about their kids' emotions had children with fewer behavior problems.
## When to check in with your pediatrician

Most tantrums are just part of growing up. Researchers say the ones worth a closer look are [unpredictable, very long or destructive](https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2012/08/kids-temper-tantrums), and studies of preschoolers with depression or behavior disorders found their tantrums were more often [violent or self-harmful, and harder to recover from](https://source.washu.edu/2007/12/excessive-tantrums-in-preschoolers-may-indicate-serious-mental-health-problems/). Talk to your pediatrician if your child:
- Often hurts themselves, other people or things during tantrums.
- Has tantrums most days in the preschool years, or they seem to come out of nowhere.
- Struggles to calm down even with your help, or tantrums are getting worse instead of better after age four.
- Or if you're worried. You know your child, and asking is always OK.
## And your big feelings?

Here's the part no one puts on the parenting charts: tantrums are hard on us too. It's OK to feel embarrassed, angry or completely done. It's OK to say "I need a minute" and take a breath (or hand off to another grown-up, as the AAP suggests).

And if you yell? Repair it. "I yelled, and I'm sorry. I was frustrated. Let's try again." That small moment teaches your child something powerful: big feelings happen to everyone, and love is still there when they pass.

You're not raising a kid who never melts down. You're raising a kid who learns, slowly and with your help, what to do when they do. That takes years, and it's happening right now, one cereal aisle at a time.

title: How to actually get a spot at library storytime
summary: Free library storytimes are the best deal around for little kids, and the good ones fill up. Five quick tips for Spring Branch and Memorial.
body: Free library storytimes are the best deal around for little kids, and the good ones fill up. Here's how to get in near Spring Branch and Memorial.
- Get there 15 minutes early. At Spring Branch Memorial Library, storytime tickets are free from the children's desk, and they can run out.
- Know there's a second session. Baby Bouncers (Wednesdays) and Tiny Tykes (Thursdays) both run at 10:15 and again at 11:15.
- Sign up ahead at Ring. Ring Neighborhood Library's toddler storytime (Wednesdays, 18 to 36 months) opens registration on the library calendar, so check it a couple of weeks out.
- Check the calendar that morning. Storytimes can be canceled on short notice. Spring Branch Memorial canceled Tiny Tykes on Oct 22 because of staffing.
- Match the age. Baby Bouncers is for crawlers and new walkers, Tiny Tykes for new walkers, and preschool storytime with a craft is for ages 3 to 6.
Every storytime near you, with times, is in the "Every week" section of our calendar.

title: Kids eat free near Spring Branch: a night-by-night cheat sheet
summary: Monday through Wednesday, there's a kids-eat-free deal near Spring Branch and Memorial every night. Here's where.
body: Dinner out with little kids adds up fast. These deals help. Most need an adult entrée, and details change, so call ahead.
- Monday: The Union Kitchen in Memorial (one free kids' meal per adult entrée) and Local Table (participating locations).
- Tuesday: The Union Kitchen again, plus Pluckers (two free kids' meals per adult entrée for kids 10 and under, dine-in), Black-eyed Pea and Dish Society.
- Wednesday: Feges BBQ in Spring Branch, where kids 12 and under eat free from 5 to 8 pm. Red Robin takes half off kids' meals at participating locations.
- Thursday to Sunday: we haven't found a reliable deal nearby yet. Know one? Reply to the newsletter and tell us.
Our pick for a full family night out is Feges: kids eat free on Wednesdays, and there's a play area and a patio.
Every deal, by day, is on our Eats page.

title: The clocks fall back Sunday. Your toddler didn't get the memo.
summary: That "extra hour" can turn a 6 am riser into a 5 am riser. What the research says about kids and the time change, and a simple plan to start this week.
imagePrompt: A cozy, realistic early-morning scene in a Houston family kitchen: a dad in a faded T-shirt holds a mug of coffee while his wide-awake preschool daughter in pajamas points out the window at the pale pink sunrise, a stuffed bunny tucked under her arm. Soft golden light through the window, warm wood cabinets, a calm and slightly sleepy, happy mood. No text, clocks with readable numbers, signs or logos.
body: If you have a vague memory of loving the end of daylight saving time, that was probably before kids. Back then, "fall back" meant an extra hour in bed. Now it can mean a small person standing by your pillow at 5 am, fully dressed, asking for pancakes.

This year the clocks go back one hour at 2 am on Sunday, November 1. Your child's body clock doesn't read the calendar. It runs on light, routine and habit, so for a few days it will keep doing exactly what it did last week, just an hour "early" on the clock.
The good news: the fall change is the easier one, the research is mostly reassuring, and you still have a few nights to get ahead of it.
## What actually happens to little kids

Picture a toddler who sleeps 7 pm to 6 am. On Sunday, their body still thinks bedtime is 7, but the clock says 6. If you hold out for 7, they're overtired and cranky. If you put them down at 6, they wake at 5. That's the whole problem in one sentence.

The fall change is gentler than the spring one, according to [the American Academy of Pediatrics' guide on HealthyChildren.org](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Daylight-Saving-Time-Dont-Lose-Sleep-Over-It.aspx), but younger kids may melt down before bedtime and wake earlier than usual. Most kids adjust within about a week.

There isn't much research on babies and toddlers in the fall, and that's worth saying out loud. The best data comes from conference abstracts, which are short early reports, not full peer-reviewed studies:

- In the fall, [a 2023 abstract that tracked sleep in 510 infants](https://drcraigcanapari.com/daylight-savings-time-and-your-child-falling-back/), summarized by Yale pediatric sleep doctor Craig Canapari, found the middle of babies' night shifted about 10 minutes earlier for a week. Babies 3 to 6 months actually woke up less at night.

- The spring change is harder. In [a 2019 abstract on 624 children up to age 2](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article-abstract/42/Supplement_1/A97/5451230), kids lost 15 to 20 minutes of night sleep at first. Toddlers' bedtimes were back to normal in about 3 days, while babies took about 8.
So, a few rough mornings? Likely. A lasting sleep disaster? Very unlikely.
## Why your worry matters too

One finding stuck with me. In [a 2024 abstract on 602 parents of babies](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/47/Supplement_1/A358/7655311), parents with more anxiety symptoms were about twice as likely to feel stressed about the time change. Their babies' sleep before the change wasn't any different. The parents just slept about 11 minutes less.
In other words, the dread can cost us more than the clock does. If you're already lying awake over Sunday, this is your permission to take it down a notch.
## The plan: nudge later, starting now

The idea is to slide your child's day a little later before Sunday, so the new clock lines up with their body. The AAP suggests moving naps and bedtime a few minutes each day, ideally starting about a week ahead.
With six nights left, here's one easy way to do it:
- Tuesday and Wednesday: bedtime 15 minutes later than usual. Push naps and meals 15 minutes later too.
- Thursday through Saturday: 30 minutes later than usual.
- Sunday: go to your normal clock bedtime. Your child's body will be only about half an hour off instead of a full hour, and they'll catch up within days.

Short on time or energy? Dr. Canapari's version is even simpler: if your child doesn't wake painfully early, you can do nothing at all. If they do, shift everything 30 minutes later for the three days before the change.
Babies and kids who struggle with any change in routine may need smaller steps over more days. Slow is fine.
## Light is your secret weapon
Light tells the body clock what time it is. After the change, mornings get brighter earlier and evenings get dark sooner, which nudges kids toward waking early. Work with it:

- Get outside in the late afternoon. A walk or playground run before dinner helps push sleepiness later. The forest-themed play area at Haden Park or the open fields at Agnes Moffitt Park are good spots, and early November in Houston is finally pleasant.
- Keep early mornings dim. Blackout curtains, no lights on, and a calm "it's still night time" if they're up before your wake time.
- Then flood the morning with light at your real wake time. Open the blinds, eat breakfast by a window.
- Dim the house an hour before bed and put screens away, which the AAP recommends anyway.
If your child is a reliable early bird already, an "OK to wake" light or a simple rule ("you can get up when the sun is up and Mom opens the curtains") can help. Expect it to take practice.
## Know how much sleep is normal

It helps to know the target. The [American Academy of Sleep Medicine's guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4877308/), which the AAP supports, recommend 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours (naps included) for babies 4 to 12 months, 11 to 14 hours for 1- and 2-year-olds, and 10 to 13 hours for kids 3 to 5.

Those are wide ranges, on purpose. If your child is in range and mostly cheerful, a week of shuffled mornings won't undo anything. If sleep problems last well beyond a couple of weeks, or your child snores loudly or seems exhausted during the day, that's a good conversation for your pediatrician. Please ask them before trying melatonin or any sleep supplement, too.
## Try this week
- Tonight or tomorrow, start moving bedtime 15 minutes later.
- Shift naps and meals along with it, so the whole day moves together.
- Plan some outdoor time in the late afternoon this week.
- Hang blackout curtains or tape up a dark sheet before Saturday night.
- Sunday morning, keep the room dark until your usual wake time, then open the blinds wide.
- Give it a week before deciding anything is "broken."

And if Sunday starts at 5 am anyway? Make the coffee, enjoy the sunrise with your little early bird, and remember that it will settle down in a few days. Their bodies are good at this. You're doing fine.

title: Your toddler screamed on Santa's lap? That's right on schedule.
summary: Fear of strangers often grows between ages 1 and 3, and a big bearded man in red is the ultimate stranger. How to plan holiday photos without a meltdown, or skip them guilt-free.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic scene in a festive outdoor shopping plaza at dusk, strung with twinkle lights and a big decorated tree in the soft-focus background. A Middle Eastern dad in his thirties with glasses and a short dark beard holds his curious 2-year-old daughter on his hip; she has curly dark hair and a red knit hat and is peeking shyly over his shoulder and smiling. Beside them, her grandmother in a long wool coat and soft scarf laughs and points toward the lights. Cozy, happy, unhurried mood. No text, signs or logos.
body: Every December, the internet fills up with the same photo: a cheerful Santa, a toddler arched backward mid-scream, and a parent just out of frame wondering if they've scarred their child for life. If that was your kid last year (or you're bracing for this year), take a breath.

A toddler who screams on Santa's lap isn't broken, spoiled or traumatized. They're doing exactly what their brain is built to do at this age. Let's talk about why, and how to plan this year's visit so it's fun, or skip it without a shred of guilt.
## Why Santa is the ultimate stranger

Think about it from a two-year-old's point of view. A huge man they've never met, with a face mostly hidden by hair, a booming voice and a strange red suit, sits in a loud, crowded place. Then the grown-ups they trust most hand them over and walk away.

That's a near-perfect recipe for stranger anxiety: the wariness, clinginess and tears that show up when a little one meets someone unfamiliar. The [Merck Manual](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/children-s-health-issues/symptoms-in-infants-and-children/separation-anxiety-and-stranger-anxiety) says it usually begins around 8 to 9 months, and that children 8 to 18 months old often get frightened when they meet new people or visit new places.
Stranger anxiety is actually a sign of healthy development. It means your child knows who their people are, and notices when someone isn't one of them.
## It doesn't always fade by two
You'll often read that stranger anxiety is over by age two. For plenty of kids, that's not how it goes.

[A study that followed 1,285 children](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4129944/) from 6 to 36 months, using parents' reports, found that on average, fear of strangers rose between 6 and 12 months, held steady until about 22 months, then rose again by 36 months. About 3 in 4 children followed a pattern where their wariness of strangers *increased* over the toddler years, either steeply or slowly.

A few honest notes: the children were twins in Wisconsin, mostly white and middle class, so it isn't the whole picture. But the takeaway is reassuring. A three-year-old who suddenly wants nothing to do with Santa, after a calm photo at one, is not going backward. They're right on track.

Every kid is different, too. In the same study, some babies started out very wary and slowly warmed up, and others stayed cautious throughout. Temperament plays a big part, and the researchers think it may be partly inherited. Your shy kid might just come by it honestly.
## How to set up a visit that might actually work

Experts who study childhood fears say the same few things help. Martin Antony, a psychology professor and anxiety researcher in Toronto, says [knowing what to expect goes a long way](https://www.newswise.com/articles/how-parents-can-help-their-kids-overcome-their-fear-of-santa), and that exposure works best when it is predictable and "under the control of the child."
- Preview Santa at home. Read picture books, look at photos and talk about what will happen: the line, the chair, the smile, the goodbye.
- Watch first. Let your child see other kids (or an older sibling) visit Santa from a distance before it's their turn.
- Go when they're rested and fed. A visit right after a nap and a snack beats one that lands during the pre-dinner meltdown window.
- Let them choose how close. Standing next to Santa, sitting on your lap beside him, or waving from a few feet away are all photos too.
- Stay in the picture. Hop in with your child. Many toddlers will happily sit next to Santa if a parent is right there.

- Bring your own calm. Lurie Children's psychologist Jonathan Pochyly notes that kids take cues from [a parent's smile and enthusiasm](https://www.luriechildrens.org/en/blog/how-to-survive-a-visit-to-santa-if-your-child-feels-anxious/) when facing something unfamiliar.

Locally, CityCentre's free Holiday in the Plaza is planned for Saturday, November 28 (the date may still change). In past years it has had Santa and photos in exchange for a donated toy. An outdoor plaza with room to watch from a distance is a gentle first try.
## The "never force it" rule

If your child is crying, reaching for you and arching away, the experts are clear: [never force it](https://www.luriechildrens.org/en/blog/how-to-survive-a-visit-to-santa-if-your-child-feels-anxious/). As Dr. Pochyly puts it, if they aren't ready, there's always next year.

Forcing a scared toddler into a stranger's arms teaches them that their "no" doesn't count, which is the opposite of what we want them to learn about their bodies. The same goes for hugs and kisses from relatives at holiday gatherings. A wave, a high five or a blown kiss is a perfectly polite greeting from a two-year-old.
Also skip the "Santa won't bring presents if you cry" line. Fear isn't misbehavior, and a threat won't help a scared kid feel any safer.
## Skipping it is fine. So is the crying photo.

Here's permission, in writing: you don't have to do a Santa photo at all. You can take a cozy picture by your own tree, mail Santa a letter instead, or wave at him across the plaza and call it a win. Antony says it's [perfectly normal for young children to be afraid of Santa](https://www.newswise.com/articles/how-parents-can-help-their-kids-overcome-their-fear-of-santa), and many kids who refuse at two are begging for a photo a few years later.
And if you do end up with the screaming photo? Some families treasure those most of all. Just let it be the photo, not a struggle to keep going until you get a smiling one.

One note: being shy with Santa is normal. The [Merck Manual](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/children-s-health-issues/symptoms-in-infants-and-children/separation-anxiety-and-stranger-anxiety) says stranger anxiety that is very intense or lasts a long time can be a sign of broader anxiety. If your child's fears get in the way of daily life, like daycare drop-off, playdates or doctor visits, mention it to your pediatrician.
## Try this week
- Find a picture book about Santa or holiday visits at the library and read it a few times.
- Look at last year's photos together and talk about Santa as a friendly helper.
- Decide your plan ahead of time, including a no-pressure "we'll just wave today" option.
- Give grandparents a heads-up that hugs are optional this year.
Your little one isn't ruining Christmas. They're learning who feels safe, and they're checking with you. That's a good thing, even when it's loud.

sources.label: Brooker RJ, Buss KA, Lemery-Chalfant K, Aksan N, Davidson RJ, Goldsmith HH. The development of stranger fear in infancy and toddlerhood: normative development, individual differences, antecedents, and outcomes. Developmental Science, 2013.
Consolini DM. Separation anxiety and stranger anxiety. Merck Manual Consumer Version, reviewed 2025.
Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago. How to help a child with a fear of visiting Santa Claus, 2023.
Newswise. Expert: how parents can help their kids overcome their fear of Santa (Martin Antony, Ryerson University), 2012.

title: 10 Birthday Party Ideas Near Spring Branch
summary: Indoor playgrounds, gyms, a pool, a nature playscape, pottery painting and a $70 park pad: where to throw a kids' birthday party near Spring Branch and Memorial.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic outdoor birthday party under a covered park picnic pavilion shaded by big live oak trees in Houston. Two moms host: a Black mom with short natural hair and a Latina mom with a long braid, both laughing as their 5-year-old son in round glasses and a paper party crown leans over a simple homemade cake with a few small kids gathered around the picnic table. A playground is soft in the background. Late-afternoon golden light, relaxed and joyful mood. No text, signs, logos or balloons.
body: If you've ever stood in your kitchen at 11 pm, frosting a cake and wondering how fifteen preschoolers will fit in your living room, this one's for you. Hosting a party at home is lovely in theory. In practice, it's a week of cleaning before and a week of finding Goldfish crackers in the couch after.

The good news: Spring Branch and Memorial are surrounded by places that will hand you a room, a host and a cleanup crew. I checked every venue below on its own website. Where a venue publishes prices, I've included rough starting points, but prices change, so always confirm with the venue before you book.
## Indoor play

- [Giggles & Fun](https://gigglesandfun.com/kids-birthday-parties-houston-tx/) on South Dairy Ashford, just southwest of Memorial, is built for little kids: its playground is designed for ages 7 and under, with toddler-friendly areas. Parties run 3 hours (2 hours in the party room and playground, plus an hour of open play) and include a party host, setup and cleanup help, and paper goods. A weekday mini party for 6 kids starts around $200, and weekend packages for 12 kids start around $325 on Sundays. Outside food is allowed for a small fee.

- [The Bunny Hive](https://www.thebunnyhive.com/houston/parties), in a bungalow on Heights Boulevard, is worth the short drive for a baby's or toddler's party. You rent the whole studio, with its soft, neutral playroom, a kids' table, a toddler bar and seating for grown-ups. A 3-hour private rental (setup and cleanup included) runs about $850, with a staff member and a sound system on hand. You can bring your own food, drinks and decorations, and a staff-led Play-Doh station is an add-on. Book at least 10 days ahead.

- [Lanky Land](https://www.lankylandtx.com/) on the Northwest Freeway, just east of Spring Branch, is an indoor playground for ages 1 to 10, with about 4,000 square feet of slides, climbing and a ball pit, plus a separate baby area for kids under 3. It has party rooms for birthdays. No party prices are posted, so ask for current packages. Grip socks are required for kids, and grown-ups on the play floor wear socks too.
## Active parties

- [The Little Gym Houston-Memorial](https://www.thelittlegym.com/texas-houston-memorial/kids-birthday-parties/) on Memorial Drive hosts birthday kids ages 1 to 12. You get about an hour in the gym and 30 minutes in a party room, two instructors, private use of the gym, paper goods, and setup and cleanup. Packages start around $395 for 15 kids. A sweet pick for a first or second birthday.

- [RISE at The Warehouse](https://risewarehouse.com/birthday-parties/) on the West Sam Houston Parkway in Spring Branch offers a gymnastics or ninja party (1.5 hours) or a combo of both (2 hours), for up to 20 kids. Packages start around $425, or $500 for the combo. The page doesn't list ages, so ask about the youngest guests if you have toddlers coming.

- [Goldfish Swim School West Houston](https://goldfishswimschool.com/west-houston/birthday-parties/), in the same Dairy Ashford center as Giggles & Fun, does indoor pool parties with private use of the pool, lifeguards, instructors who lead games, decorations, cupcakes and drinks. All ages can join, but kids who can't swim on their own need a grown-up in the water. No prices are published, so call for a quote. A warm pool in January is a very good trick to have.

- [Urban Air Houston Heights](https://www.urbanair.com/texas-houston-heights/kids-birthday-parties/), off I-10 a short drive east of Spring Branch, is the burn-all-the-energy option. Two-hour parties include a reserved table, a shared host, every attraction and grip socks. A Small Squad party for 5 guests starts around $200, and packages for 10 start around $400. Some attractions have height limits, so it's usually a better fit for bigger kids than for toddlers.
## Outdoors and nature

- [The Houston Arboretum & Nature Center](https://houstonarboretum.org/facilities/birthday-parties/) rents parts of its Nature Playscape for 2-hour parties on weekend mornings and afternoons, with one free add-on activity. Packages start around $315 for 15 kids and go up to 40 kids. A few things to know: you need a Family Tree membership or higher to book, there are no parties June through August, and balloons, piñatas and outside vendors aren't allowed. Plan on 1 grown-up for every 5 kids.

- [Memorial Park](https://www.memorialparkconservancy.org/visit/reservations/picnic-areas-pavilions/) rents covered pavilions in 3-hour blocks, starting around $250 on weekdays for up to 50 people, with higher weekend rates. Bring your own everything, and leave the bounce house and balloons at home: both are prohibited.
## Creative

- [The Mad Potter Memorial](https://themadpotter.com/pages/kids-parties-memorial), now on Fountain View Drive near San Felipe, runs 2-hour pottery painting parties with a party host, a decorated table, games and prizes. Packages start around $399 for 8 painters, plus a 15% host gratuity, and the top package adds cake and pizza. Great for preschoolers and big kids who like to make something with their own hands.
## Budget-friendly

- The best deal on this list: Memorial Park's [covered picnic pads at the Vale-Asche playground](https://www.memorialparkconservancy.org/visit/reservations/picnic-areas-pavilions/), made for kids' gatherings, start around $70 for up to 30 people, with a covered table and the playground right there.

- Unreserved picnic areas at Memorial Park are first-come, first-served and free. Free neighborhood parks like Haden Park and Agnes Moffitt Park in Spring Branch work too, if someone can get there early to claim a table.
- Small parties cost less. Giggles & Fun's weekday mini party and Urban Air's Small Squad are both built for about 5 or 6 kids.
## Tips before you book
- Book 4 to 6 weeks ahead. The Arboretum needs at least two weeks and Memorial Park at least seven days, but the most popular dates and times usually go well before that.
- Weekend slots go first. Saturday mornings disappear fastest. A Sunday or a Friday afternoon is often easier to get, and at some places it's cheaper.

- Ask exactly what's included. How long is the party? How many kids are included, and what does each extra child cost? Do grown-ups count? Can you bring outside food and cake? Is there a deposit, a host gratuity or a cancellation fee?

- Have a heat and rain plan. Houston weather can turn hot or stormy fast, in almost any month. For an outdoor party, pick a covered spot, bring a cooler of water and plan for shade. Ask about the weather policy before you pay (the Arboretum, for one, may offer a partial refund or reschedule in extreme weather).
- Match the venue to the kid. A shy 3-year-old may love a small party at a playscape more than a loud trampoline park, and a big crowd isn't required for a big day.
## The part that actually matters

Your kid will not remember the party favors or whether the cake came from a bakery or the grocery store. They'll remember that their friends came, that someone sang to them, and that you were there. Pick the place that fits your budget and your sanity, book it, and then go enjoy the cake.

title: Screen-time guilt? The research is kinder than you think.
summary: What pediatricians actually recommend for babies through age 6, why what they watch beats how long, and simple ways to make screen time calmer (meltdown included).
imagePrompt: A candid, cozy photo of a white 2-year-old boy with tousled light-brown hair, in dinosaur pajamas, sitting cross-legged on a soft rug and watching a tablet propped against a couch cushion, totally absorbed, the screen's glow on his face. Warm afternoon window light, a few toys scattered nearby, plain wall above him. The screen faces away from the camera so nothing on it shows. No logos or brand names.
body: If you're reading this while a cartoon plays in the next room so you can finally eat lunch sitting down, welcome. You're not ruining your kid. You're a parent in 2026.

Screen time might be the topic with the most guilt per square inch. The rules sound strict, the headlines sound scary, and real life has sick days, rainy afternoons and a baby who only naps in the car.
So let's look at what the experts actually say, what the research really shows, and how to make screens work for your family without the shame spiral.
## What the AAP and WHO actually recommend

In January 2026, the American Academy of Pediatrics [replaced its older media guidance](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/news-releases/aap/2026/american-academy-of-pediatrics-calls-for-creating-a-child-friendly-digital-world/) with a new policy. It moves away from one strict rule for everyone and toward limits that fit each family. Here's the gist for little kids, from [the full policy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13122503/):

- **Babies under about 18 months:** They have a hard time taking what they see on a screen and using it in real life. Babies don't learn from videos, but the AAP says an occasional short, high-quality video isn't harmful.
- **Toddlers and preschoolers:** For entertainment shows and apps, the AAP suggests a limit that might be under 1 hour a day, worked out around your family's routine.

- **Video chat is different.** Calling Grandma counts as real back-and-forth conversation. The AAP [suggests video chatting with family](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/media-and-children/center-of-excellence-on-social-media-and-youth-mental-health/qa-portal/qa-portal-library/qa-portal-library-questions/screen-time-for-infants/) and helping little ones by explaining who's on the screen and what they're saying.

The World Health Organization is a bit stricter. Its [2019 guidelines](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2019-to-grow-up-healthy-children-need-to-sit-less-and-play-more) say screen time isn't recommended for babies under 1 or for 1-year-olds, and that 2- to 4-year-olds should have no more than 1 hour a day, with "less is better."
Notice what both have in common: these are goals, not grades. Most families land somewhere in the middle on most days.
## What they watch (and who's watching) matters more than the minutes

[A 2020 review of 42 studies with about 18,900 children](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7091394/) found that more screen time was linked with slightly weaker language skills. But educational shows and co-viewing (a grown-up watching along and chatting about it) were linked with slightly *stronger* language skills. These were small effects and the studies can't prove cause, but the direction is encouraging.

Pace matters too. In [a small experiment with 60 four-year-olds](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9923845/), kids who watched just 9 minutes of a very fast-paced cartoon did worse right afterward on tasks that test self-control, focus and following steps than kids who watched a slower educational show or drew pictures.

The AAP's policy points to calmer, high-quality shows, with nonprofits like PBS KIDS and Sesame Workshop as examples, and suggests skipping content packed with ads, rewards and constant flashing action.
## Background TV and screens before bed
Two habits are worth a closer look, because changing them is pretty painless.

**Background TV.** In [a 2009 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19487612/), 329 kids ages 2 months to 4 years wore small recorders all day. For each hour a TV was audible, the women around them spoke about 636 fewer words, and the kids made fewer sounds and had fewer back-and-forth exchanges. The same [2020 review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7091394/) linked background TV with weaker language skills. The easy fix: when nobody's watching, turn it off and play music or a podcast instead, if you like the noise.

**Screens before bed.** In [a survey of 715 UK parents](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5390665/) of kids 6 to 36 months, each extra hour of daily tablet use was linked with 15.6 minutes less sleep overall. It's a snapshot, so it can't show which came first, but it fits with the AAP's advice to stop screens an hour before bed and keep devices out of bedrooms. If your child falls asleep to videos, the AAP suggests a sound machine or quiet music as a swap.
## Realistic strategies for busy parents

- **Make a simple plan together.** The AAP's free [Family Media Plan](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/fmp/Pages/MediaPlan.aspx) walks you through when, where and what. Even two or three house rules count.

- **Pick a few screen-free zones.** The AAP suggests [the car and the dinner table](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/news-releases/aap/2026/american-academy-of-pediatrics-calls-for-creating-a-child-friendly-digital-world/). Car-seat time can be for songs, "I spy" and staring out the window. (The policy does say a tablet on a long road trip or plane ride is fine.)
- **Watch together when you can.** Even a few minutes of "How do you think she feels right now?" turns a show into a conversation.
- **Choose slower shows.** Gentle pace, real-life stories, few ads. If it feels frantic to you, it probably is.
- **Plan the off switch.** End at the end of an episode, not mid-scene. Give a heads-up ("one more, then snack"), let your child press the button, and have the next thing ready.

- **Have other calm-down tools, too.** The AAP notes that when screens become the main way a child calms down, kids get fewer chances to practice handling big feelings. A show on a rough day is fine. Just keep a few other options in rotation, like a cuddle, a bath or a snack on the porch.
- **Put your own phone down sometimes.** Kids notice what we do more than what we say. (This one's for all of us.)
## Let go of the guilt

Guilt doesn't help anyone watch better shows. A tired parent who turns on a calm, gentle show so they can shower is meeting a real need. The research is about patterns over months, not one long sick day in front of the TV.
If you have concerns about your child's speech, sleep, behavior or how much they rely on screens, bring it up with your pediatrician. That's exactly what they're there for.
## Try this week
- Turn off the background TV for one afternoon and notice how it feels.
- Pick one screen-free zone, like dinner or short car rides.
- Watch one episode with your child and talk about it.
- Move the last screen of the day to at least an hour before bed.
You're not aiming for zero. You're aiming for screens that fit your family, plus plenty of laps, books and back-and-forth chatter. You're already doing more of that than you think.

points.heading: Babies: video chat is different.

points.heading: Pick slower, quality shows.
points.text: In one study, 9 minutes of a fast-paced cartoon left 4-year-olds worse at focus and self-control right after.

points.heading: Turn off background TV.
points.text: For each hour a TV was audible, kids heard fewer words and had fewer back-and-forth exchanges.

points.heading: Plan the off switch.
points.text: End with the episode, give a heads-up, have the next thing ready, and stop screens an hour before bed.

instagram.caption:
The most useful screen-time question isn't "how many minutes?" It's "what, and with whom?"

In a review of 42 studies, educational shows and watching together were linked with slightly stronger language skills. Background TV and lots of screen time were linked with weaker ones.

Easy wins: turn the TV off when nobody's watching, choose slower shows, make dinner and the car screen-free, and stop screens an hour before bed. Video calls with Grandma? Those count as conversation.

And please drop the guilt. One long sick day on the couch isn't a pattern.
